story|title:amd and intel s ai compute e.content_excerpt: The rival chipmakers' joint ACEv1 specification promises 16x matrix compute density over existing instructions, with hardware support expected no earlier than 2028 AMD and Intel, two companies that have spent decades trying to eat each other’s lunch, just co-authored the recipe. Their shared AI Compute Extensions specification, known as ACEv1, has been merged into the GCC 17 development branch as of September 2, 2026, bringing standardized AI acceleration capabilities to the world’s most widely used open-source compiler toolchain. The move represents a rare moment of genuine technical cooperation between the x86 duopoly, and it carries implications well beyond compiler flags. In a computing landscape increasingly dominated by Arm-based designs and purpose-built AI accelerators, AMD and Intel are betting that a unified approach to matrix computation can keep the x86 architecture relevant for the next decade of AI workloads. At its core, ACEv1 introduces a matrix acceleration architecture optimized for AI and machine learning tasks. The specification uses outer-product instructions to deliver up to 16 times the compute density compared to equivalent AVX10 operations. The standard supports a range of low-precision numerical formats including INT8, FP8, and BF16. These formats matter because most AI inference workloads don’t need the full precision of traditional floating-point math. ACEv1 builds on concepts from Intel’s Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX), which shipped in the company’s Sapphire Rapids server chips. But there’s a crucial distinction: ACEv1 is not backward-compatible with AMX. The specification was first published in June 2026 through the x86 Ecosystem Advisory Group, an industry body that AMD and Intel formed in 2024 specifically to tackle standardization challenges. Engineers from both companies contributed the compiler patches that landed in GCC 17’s development branch on September 2. Full GCC support is expected to arrive with the GCC 17.1 release, projected for March to April 2027. No hardware implementing ACEv1 is anticipated before 2028, with AMD hinting that these AI features could appear in its upcoming Zen 7 processor architecture. The lack of backward compatibility with Intel’s AMX signals that both companies decided a fresh start was more valuable than preserving legacy code paths. story|title:building a better dependabot.content_excerpt: dependabot · renovate · dependency management · ai agents · cloudflare workers · durable objects · github Felix was built with a lot of help from Claude Code, and I used an LLM to help organize this post. The opinions (and the grudges against Dependabot) are my own. Here are two pull requests for the same Rust upgrade on my Rust template repository. Dependabot’s bumped the rust image in the Dockerfile but not rust-toolchain.toml alongside it. The other one bumped both pins together, explained why it didn’t touch the rust-version MSRV in Cargo.toml , and listed what changed upstream in 1.100 that could affect the repo. That one came from Felix. Dependabot promised to automate away a chore many of us skipped because of the tedious, never-ending onslaught of updates, and when it launched, people loved it. Years later, I have a bad case of what I call dependency burnout. Dependabot bumps something, the build breaks, and now fixing it is my problem. Multiply that across every repo and I just stopped merging them altogether unless I needed a bugfix or a new feature. Meanwhile, the steady stream of new CVEs and zero-days has made keeping dependencies up to date more important than ever. And Dependabot hasn’t really kept up. The alternatives don’t always fare better in practice, either. At my $DAYJOB we use Renovate , but it’s been dialed way back. It only runs once a week and the rebase commands are turned off, so its PRs go stale and start conflicting before anyone gets to them. So I built Felix. The name is a nod to Fix-It Felix Jr. from Wreck-It Ralph , because the whole point is that it fixes things, and doesn’t just bump numbers and walk away. Dependabot, Renovate, and the rest of the update bots are rigid in their approach. Find all the Cargo.toml , package.json , requirements.txt and lockfiles, check upstream for new versions, and if anything changed, update the manifest and lockfile and open a pull request. The main campaign, Mir2k, hides a Windows remote access trojan at the end of GGUF files and later arms the chat template to make the model print the command that unpacks it. Local LLMs are usually shared as GGUF files, and every GGUF file carries a chat template that the runtime applies to each prompt. Chat template poisoning abuses that template. The model answers normally, while the template quietly adds instructions the user never sees: make an agent run a PowerShell command, or open every reply with a command for the user to run. In its strongest form, the malicious program travels inside the model file itself, appended after the last tensor where loaders never read, and the template is switched on later. A scan of all 3273389 public Hugging Face model repositories on 26 November 2026 found 5 malicious GGUF models with 2428 downloads as of 27 November. Hugging Face counts downloads, not people, so the number of affected users is lower or equal. The largest campaign, Mir2k , uploaded two uncensored GGUF models with a Windows remote access trojan named ollie hidden at the end of each file, and on 26 November rewrote both templates so the model asks the user to run the line that unpacks it. The open-source tool gguf-radar detects these templates and hidden bytes without running anything, and rebuilds a clean GGUF file with the model weights unchanged. I think this is the first major product that's attempting to tax agentic use cases. I'm not sure it will work. Effectively two things. Firstly, all agents need to use MCP, not API to interact with Google. Quite how they plan on enforcing this I'm not sure, as the best I suspect they can do is behavioural profiling of what APIs get called, which seems to be quite difficult. I strongly believe this is mostly targeted at large AI companies and not smaller developers or solo users; but it is likely to have serious impact on any company that is (or will) start integrating agentic workflows into their products. Secondly, a new pricing tier for said MCPs. In true Google style it's complicated, but in essence it's a charge per 1000 requests , with different types of requests using different pricing tiers. Roughly speaking, you can read 1000 emails via MCP for $0.20. There is a free tier of 5,000 calls a day, but this is grouped across all access for a specific Google Cloud project. story|title:what it takes to let ai agen.content_excerpt: Letting AI agents work unattended is safe when the rules are set up before you leave. A practical look at planning, sandboxing, testing and reviewing their work. The concern is warranted. There are plenty of stories of AI building fragile software with glaring security holes . Agents have also made reckless decisions on their own, like dropping a production database . It’s sensible to be wary, but don’t dismiss the idea. With the right guardrails and practices in place, you can safely hand work to agents and step away while they do it, shipping high-quality software at a much faster pace. Even in security-sensitive environments, the same approach applies, although you need to be deliberate about where the agent runs and what code leaves your network. The catch is that the effort doesn’t disappear with asynchronous agents. It shifts to planning before the agent starts and reviewing what it produces. In this article, I’ll cover what it takes to work with asynchronous agents safely and get quality output from them. I won’t compare particular tools or models, since these advance quickly. Instead, I’ll focus on concepts and practices that apply regardless of harness (the tool that runs the agent) and model. Any tools I do mention are just examples I’ve used myself. Most developers started out using AI for coding in a chat window, either in the browser or as a side panel in their IDE. When these chat tools first arrived, they were mind-blowing. AI agents, though, are so much more than a simple chat interface. An agent can read context, make decisions, and take actions on your behalf, like writing code or debugging an application. How you work with an agent can be synchronous or asynchronous. In a synchronous setup, you watch the agent work in real time, answering its questions and steering it as it goes. In an asynchronous setup, you hand it a task and walk away. You come back to a pull request that’s ready for review. Removing that hands-on control lets you scale your effort by running multiple agents in parallel, so you can get through far more work in the same amount of time. Working asynchronously changes what the quality of the resulting code depends on. When you work synchronously, you’re the safety net. You notice the agent drifting, correct it mid-task, and catch mistakes as they happen. story|variant:image|title:code driven ai.content_excerpt: An interesting trend in frontier LLMs released in the second half of 2026 is that they tend to be much better at visual reasoning and creative “design” than their predecessors. If you ask these text-output models to create a 2D image (or a 3D model, as discussed here previously ), you’re very likely to get a useful result, and you may even get one that’s aesthetically impressive. Most importantly, because these images are defined using code you (or the model) can make further edits to them without any of the weirdness that comes from iterating with a text-input, image-output model. Gemini 4 Neon is getting some buzz for its 2D design skills, so I decided to try it out in AI Studio starting with the prompt: Create an SVG poster promoting the Kakapo recovery project, research details first, make the poster look really cool and give it a 1970s graphic design It took some iteration, partly because AI Studio doesn’t render SVGs, so the models there can’t spot visual mistakes without assistance. Make the kakapo a bit more realistic, especially the face (image search for references) Here’s the full transcript , exported from AI Studio as Markdown because I couldn’t find a way to share a session that didn’t require a Google login to view. AI Studio ran Google searches to find those numbers—I’ve checked and they are all correct. I like that it included red rimu tree fruit on the branch, since those are essential for the breeding season . Whether or not you like the poster, the key thing about it is that everything is editable . You can directly edit the text in the SVG, or you can open it in Inkscape or Adobe Illustrator or Boxy SVG and edit it visually. I have a well documented fondness for SVG generation, but it’s not the only game in town. A model hooked up to a coding agent environment can execute code to generate images. This opens up a whole realm of possibilities—generated image files, HTML and CSS, 2D HTML Canvas elements, Blender scripts, WebGPU shaders, PDF... any image mechanism that can be represented by a file on disk or the output of a script can be targeted by a model with a coding agent. One of the reasons vibe game development has exploded recently is that models like Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Neon are capable of creating good-enough quality game assets—3D models, textures, sprites, etc—entirely through writing code.
